results.result: VHH123 and VHH188 are specific for mouse and human TfR, respectively, with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface proteins as demonstrated by immunoblot, LC/MS/MS, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins, and flow cytometry. Contaminants co-immunoprecipitated were predominantly cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins not accessible in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 provide convergent evidence from multiple orthogonal methods (immunoblot, LC/MS/MS, SDS-PAGE, flow cytometry) demonstrating specificity. C67-C68 address potential contamination concerns and appropriately dismiss them based on subcellular localization. The multi-method validation approach is rigorous and the conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: Anti-TfR nanobodies enable non-invasive tracking of transplanted cells by PET/CT without genetic modification. VHH123 tracks mouse cells in Tfrchu/hu recipients, while VHH188 tracks Tfrchu/hu cells in C57BL/6 recipients. The congenic mouse pair with species-specific VHHs provides a unique tool for transplant studies of any TfR-expressing proliferating cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C112 provide direct experimental evidence of bone marrow transplant tracking with appropriate controls (C109). The timing considerations (C111) and feasibility conclusions (C112) are well-supported by the data. Claims C122-C124 and C154-C155 appropriately summarize the utility of the system. This represents a core finding of the manuscript.

results.result: 89Zr and 64Cu chelated to anti-TfR nanobodies are released upon endocytosis due to exposure to low endosomal pH. At later timepoints (≥24 hr), PET signals predominantly reflect free radioisotope accumulation in mineralized bone (89Zr) rather than TfR distribution. This release is unique to anti-TfR VHHs and not observed with VHHs targeting other surface markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 provide strong evidence from matched vs. unmatched VHH/mouse pairs, ex vivo measurements of flushed bone marrow vs. bone matrix, and ROI analysis. C84-C85 provide critical negative controls with non-TfR VHHs. C86-C88 establish the pH-dependent mechanism in vitro. The conclusion (C101, C104) that isotope release is an unavoidable consequence of TfR binding is well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: Comparison of 89Zr, 64Cu, and 18F-labeled anti-TfR VHHs reveals distinct kinetics and signal patterns. At 1 hr post-injection, all three isotopes show specific bone marrow accumulation. 18F provides sharper images but has limited observation window (<12 hr) due to short half-life. 64Cu shows liver accumulation at later timepoints due to slow release from NOTA. Isotope choice must consider target tissues and experimental time scale.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 provide systematic comparison of three radioisotopes with appropriate time-course imaging. C92-C95 correctly identify the trade-off between image quality and observation window for 18F. C96-C97 document 64Cu-specific liver accumulation with mechanistic explanation. C102-C103 provide quantitative ROI analysis supporting the conclusions. C105 appropriately summarizes practical implications.

results.result: VHH123 can image B16.F10 melanoma cells transplanted into Tfrchu/hu recipients. At 4 weeks post-transplantation, clear lung signals were observed with VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu, significantly higher than non-specific anti-GFP control. Necropsy confirmed melanotic tumors in lungs. ROI analysis on lung and heart is less precise due to breathing and cardiac motion.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 provide direct evidence of tumor detection with appropriate negative control (C116) and necropsy confirmation (C117). C113-C114 establish expected timeline. C118 shows significant difference by ROI analysis. C120-C121 appropriately acknowledge limitations of lung imaging due to motion artifacts. The tumor tracking application is well-demonstrated.

results.result: VHH188 produces intense signal in placentas of C57BL/6 mice carrying Tfrchu/wt embryos, but not in embryonic tissues. TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter fetal tissue. Notably, no free 89Zr release was observed in placenta, departing from all other imaging experiments. This may reflect unique pH conditions or absence of release co-factors in syncytiotrophoblast-I.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 provide strong evidence with appropriate controls (C128) and statistical significance (C129). C132 confirms signal originates from placenta, not embryo, through ex vivo imaging. C133-C134 document the surprising absence of 89Zr release. C178-C180 offer plausible mechanistic hypotheses but acknowledge uncertainty. The placental barrier finding is novel and well-documented, though the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Anti-TfR radiotracers show no observable CNS accumulation by PET/CT but demonstrate CNS accumulation by ex vivo radiospectrometry. The lack of PET signal is attributed to low CNS concentrations (1-5% of plasma), radioisotope release post-internalization, and potential impediment by PEGylation. Gamma ray spectrometry confirmed accumulation in CNS of appropriate genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C80-C81 clearly document the discrepancy between PET imaging and ex vivo measurements. C82 cites prior work supporting BBB crossing capability. C83 and C164-C167 provide plausible explanations for the negative PET signal. C168 provides confirmatory ex vivo data. The conclusion that VHHs cross the BBB but at levels below PET detection threshold is well-supported.

results.result: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F through click chemistry avoids radioisotope release complications but comes with trade-offs including short half-life (<12 hr observation window), expensive synthesis, and typical accumulation in elimination organs (gall bladder, GI tract) when using TCO-tetrazine chemistry.
results.evaluation: Claims C60 and C183 correctly identify the advantage of covalent 18F labeling. C61 and C184 appropriately document the limitations with supporting citations. The trade-off analysis is balanced and well-supported by both the current data and cited literature.

results.result: Nanobodies offer superior properties for PET imaging compared to intact immunoglobulins, including small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, shorter circulatory half-life (~30 min vs. several days), and improved signal-to-noise ratio. PEGylation further improves contrast by reducing renal clearance. Chemo-enzymatic methods enable site-specific modification with chelators and click handles.
results.evaluation: These claims summarize well-established advantages of nanobodies for imaging applications, appropriately supported by citations (C30-C32, C147-C148, C150-C151). The properties are stated as general knowledge in the field rather than novel findings of this study. All claims are properly referenced.

results.result: Current cell tracking methods have various limitations: fluorescence/luminescence methods suffer from limited depth penetration and require invasive surgery for cellular resolution; NMR lacks specificity; SPECT/PET lack single-cell resolution but enable non-invasive whole-body imaging. Methods for detecting tumors of mouse origin in their natural host are limited. Most approaches require genetic modification or cell-specific markers.
results.evaluation: These claims provide appropriate background context for the study, summarizing limitations of existing methods. All claims are properly supported by citations (C16-C24, C137, C139-C142, C152). C153 correctly identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current work. This represents standard literature review rather than novel findings.

results.result: TfR (CD71, encoded by Tfrc) is a homodimeric type-II transmembrane protein near-ubiquitously expressed, particularly on proliferating cells including many tumors. TfR mediates iron uptake through transferrin endocytosis and recycling. TfR is expressed at the BBB and placental barrier for iron delivery. Anti-TfR nanobodies can traverse the BBB, but placental crossing has not been explored.
results.evaluation: These claims provide essential background on TfR biology, all appropriately supported by citations (C37-C40, C47-C48). C41-C43 describe the well-established TfR trafficking pathway. C44-C46 document TfR expression at barrier sites with proper citations. C49 correctly identifies a knowledge gap addressed by the study. This represents accurate literature review.

results.result: The Tfrchu/hu mouse model (Jackson Labs strain 038212) expresses a chimeric TfR with human ectodomain (amino acids 196-381, 74% identity to mouse). Combined with species-specific anti-TfR VHHs, this constitutes a congenic pair ideally suited for transplant experiments. The system enables tracking of mouse tumors in Tfrchu/hu mice and human PDX models in wild-type mice without genetic modification. Production of nanobody tracers is relatively simple.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C62, and C163 provide specific details about the mouse model with proper citations. C158-C162 appropriately describe the advantages and applications of the system. C187-C188 make reasonable claims about accessibility and utility. The characterization of the model and its applications is well-supported.

results.result: The mechanism of 89Zr release may involve a TfR-specific co-factor beyond acidic pH. Release of free 89Zr from DFO after epitope-binding should be a concern for clinical development. The 'free 89Zr signal pattern' may be traded for increased liver signal by using 64Cu instead.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C176 are explicitly speculative ("may also be consistent," "perhaps," "may shed further light"). C175 proposes an unidentified co-factor without direct evidence. C181 makes a reasonable extrapolation to clinical applications. C182 offers a practical alternative supported by cited literature. The mechanistic speculation is acknowledged as uncertain by the authors.

results.result: VHH123 and VHH188 are species-specific nanobodies that bind only to their appropriate TfR (mouse and human, respectively) with no obvious cross-reactivity to other surface-expressed proteins, as demonstrated by immunoblot, LC/MSMS analysis, SDS-PAGE of 35S-labeled proteins, and flow cytometry.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the specificity of the nanobodies. The editor states the evidence is 'compelling,' and reviewers describe the work as presenting 'interesting data' with 'transparent' reporting. No reviewer challenges the specificity claims or the methods used to establish them.

results.result: Anti-TfR nanobodies can track transplanted cells (bone marrow, tumor cells) non-invasively by PET/CT without genetic modification. The combination of VHH123/VHH188 with Tfrchu/hu mice constitutes a congenic pair ideally suited for transplant experiments, enabling detection of transplanted bone marrow cells and their hematopoietic descendants.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this as a major contribution. The editor calls it 'highly innovative' and an 'important novel asset.' Reviewers describe it as a 'unique set of PET tracer and mouse strain' that is 'first-in-kind' and could 'facilitate cell tracking in different research fields.' No concerns are raised about the transplant tracking data.

results.result: Chelation of 89Zr and 64Cu radioisotopes to anti-TfR nanobodies results in radioisotope release upon endocytosis due to exposure to low endosomal pH. At later timepoints, strong PET signals in long bone extremities are predominantly due to accumulation of free 89Zr in mineralized bone matrix rather than bone marrow accumulation of intact tracer.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant methodological concerns, noting that 'the authors used DFO, which is well known to leak Zr, rather than the current standard for 89Zr PET which is DFO* (DFO-star).' This suggests the observed release may be a methodological artifact rather than a biological finding specific to TfR internalization. The authors are 'congratulated for presenting results that may not have turned out the way they had hoped,' implying the isotope release was unexpected and potentially problematic.

results.result: Anti-TfR radiotracers do not show observable accumulation in the CNS by PET/CT but show evidence of CNS accumulation by radiospectrometry. The lack of PET signal may be due to low CNS concentrations, radioisotope release post-internalization, and PEGylation impeding transcytosis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies critical methodological limitations: 'The brain tissues were not capillary depleted, which limits interpretation. Capillary depletion, with quantitative assessment of the completion of the depletion process, is the standard in the field.' Additionally, 'The authors have not experimentally tested the hypothesis that the PEG adduct reduced BBB transcytosis.' The reviewer concludes this is 'a surprising and somewhat disappointing finding' and that 'additional work will be needed before nanobody-based brain PET becomes feasible.'

results.result: VHH188 produces an intense signal in the placenta of C57BL/6 mice impregnated by Tfrchu/hu males, showing that TfR-specific VHHs accumulate at the placental barrier but do not enter fetal tissue. Despite strong placental accumulation, no sign of free 89Zr release was seen, departing from other imaging experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The results in Fig. 7 [actually Fig. 8] involving the placenta are interesting, but need confirmation using constructs with 18F labeling and without the PEG adduct.' This indicates the placental findings are preliminary and require additional validation with alternative labeling strategies before the conclusions can be firmly established.

results.result: Covalent modification of VHHs with 18F avoids release of free radioisotope and provides sharper images, but the short half-life of 18F limits the observation window to <12 hr. At 1 hr post-injection, all three isotopes (89Zr, 64Cu, 18F) show strong PET signal in bone marrow locations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the 18F labeling data or the trade-offs described. The comparative isotope data at early timepoints is presented as part of the overall characterization of the imaging agents, and no specific concerns are raised about these findings.

results.result: For 64Cu-labeled agents, bone marrow signal remains weakly visible at 24 hr post-injection, but liver and gut signals increase at later timepoints, attributed to slow release of 64Cu from NOTA to plasma proteins. The 'free 89Zr signal pattern' may be traded for increased liver signal by shifting to 64Cu as PET isotope.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the 64Cu kinetics data. The observation that 64Cu shows different biodistribution patterns than 89Zr is presented as part of the isotope comparison, and no specific methodological concerns are raised about these findings.

results.result: VHH123-PEG-NOTA-64Cu can detect B16.F10 melanoma lung metastases in Tfrchu/hu mice at 4 weeks post-inoculation. VHH123 gave significantly higher signal in whole lungs compared to non-specific control VHHEnh, though the difference in hyperdense tumor tissue was not significant.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the tumor imaging data. The ability to track tumor cells is presented as part of the overall utility of the system, and the editor notes the method 'could potentially facilitate cell tracking in different research fields,' which would include tumor tracking.

results.result: Choice of isotopes for anti-TfR nanobodies must be made with respect to tissues to be visualized and time scale of experiment. Release of free 89Zr from DFO after epitope-binding should be a concern in development of 89Zr-DFO radio-conjugates for clinical use. Timing of tracer injection and PET imaging is critical to avoid confounding effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a significant safety concern: 'If this line of investigation were to be translated to humans, an important consideration would be the relative safety of 89Zr and 64Cu. It is likely to be quite a bit worse than for 18F, since the 89Zr and 64Cu have longer half-lives, dissociate from their chelators, and lodge in off-target tissues.' This suggests the practical recommendations may be limited by fundamental safety issues.

results.result: Nanobodies have advantages over intact immunoglobulins including small size (~15 kDa), superior tissue penetration, shorter circulatory half-life (~30 min vs. several days), and yield images of superior quality. PEGylation further improves contrast by reducing renal clearance rate.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the advantages of nanobodies. Reviewer 1 states 'The topic of nanobody-based PET imaging is important, and holds great potential for real-world applications since nanobodies have many advantages over full sized immunoglobulins and small molecules.' The editor notes the method 'might facilitate overcoming certain limitations of alternative approaches, such as full sized immunoglobulins.'

results.result: Non-invasive tracking of specific cell types in vivo is desirable in biomedical research. Current methods include luminescence and fluorescence approaches with various limitations (depth, resolution, invasiveness), while SPECT and PET offer non-invasive whole-body imaging but lack single-cell resolution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the background context about imaging methods and their limitations. This is standard field knowledge that provides motivation for the study.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on nanobody specificity (C1, C2, C51, C52, C63-C66). Both evaluations find the multi-method validation approach compelling and well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from orthogonal methods; peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'compelling' with 'transparent' reporting. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on bone marrow transplant tracking as a major contribution (C3, C106-C112, C122-C124, C154-C155). Both evaluations recognize this as a core finding. OpenEval finds the experimental evidence and controls rigorous; peer reviewers call it 'highly innovative,' 'first-in-kind,' and an 'important novel asset.' Complete alignment on this being well-supported.

Significant disagreement on isotope release findings (C4, C74-C79, C85-C88, C101, C104, C169-C171). OpenEval finds the conclusion well-supported by converging evidence from matched/unmatched pairs and pH-dependent mechanisms. Peer Reviewer 2 raises critical methodological concerns about using DFO instead of DFO* (DFO-star), suggesting the release may be a methodological artifact rather than a biological finding. This represents a fundamental challenge to the interpretation.

Agreement that BBB crossing is uncertain but disagreement on evidence quality (C10-C11, C80-C83, C164-C168). OpenEval finds the conclusion that VHHs cross BBB at sub-PET levels well-supported by ex vivo data. Peer Reviewer 2 identifies critical methodological limitations: lack of capillary depletion and untested PEG hypothesis. Peer review considers this 'disappointing' and requiring 'additional work,' indicating lower confidence than OpenEval.

Disagreement on placental barrier findings (C8-C9, C127-C129, C132-C134, C156-C157, C177). OpenEval finds the placental barrier finding 'novel and well-documented' with strong evidence and appropriate controls, though mechanism remains speculative. Peer Reviewer 2 considers results 'interesting, but need confirmation using constructs with 18F labeling and without the PEG adduct,' indicating the findings are preliminary and require additional validation.

Agreement on tumor tracking application (C6-C7, C113-C121). Both evaluations support the tumor detection findings. OpenEval finds the evidence well-demonstrated with appropriate controls and necropsy confirmation. Peer reviewers do not challenge the tumor imaging data and include it as part of the system's utility for 'cell tracking in different research fields.'

Agreement on 18F labeling trade-offs (C60-C61, C183-C184). Both evaluations support the analysis of covalent 18F labeling advantages and limitations. OpenEval finds the trade-off analysis balanced and well-supported; peer reviewers do not challenge these findings. Complete alignment on this characterization.

Partial overlap on isotope comparison. OpenEval R4 addresses systematic comparison of three radioisotopes (C89-C98, C102-C103, C105) including 18F trade-offs and 64Cu liver accumulation. Peer R6 addresses only the 18F aspects (C89-C90, C92, C94-C95, C183-C184) without challenging the data. Agreement on the portions that overlap.

Partial overlap on 64Cu kinetics (C96-C98, C102-C103). OpenEval R4 includes 64Cu-specific liver accumulation as part of systematic isotope comparison. Peer R7 does not challenge the 64Cu biodistribution data. Agreement on these specific findings, though peer review does not extensively comment.

Strong agreement on nanobody advantages (C30-C36, C145-C151). Both evaluations support the well-established advantages of nanobodies for imaging. OpenEval notes these are properly referenced general knowledge; peer reviewers affirm nanobodies have 'many advantages' and 'great potential for real-world applications.' Complete alignment on background context.

Agreement on background literature review (C14-C29, C136-C144, C152-C153). Both evaluations support the background context about imaging method limitations. OpenEval finds all claims properly cited and representing standard literature review; peer reviewers do not challenge this background. Complete alignment on contextual claims.

Disagreement on practical recommendations and safety (C105, C111, C181). OpenEval R13 addresses mechanistic speculation (C174-C176, C181-C182) and finds it appropriately uncertain. Peer R9 raises significant safety concerns about 89Zr and 64Cu for human translation due to longer half-lives and off-target tissue accumulation, suggesting practical recommendations may be limited by fundamental safety issues not adequately addressed.

OpenEval R11 addresses TfR biology background (C37-C49, C13) finding it well-cited and accurate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers did not specifically comment on the TfR background claims.

OpenEval R12 addresses mouse model characterization and applications (C50, C53, C62, C158-C163, C187-C188) finding it well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers did not specifically challenge these characterization claims, though C158 appears in peer R2 context of overall system utility.
